Michael Sattler
mī´kel săt´lẽr
n. (Michael Sattler, c. 1490–1527, former Benedictine prior who drafted the Schleitheim Confession of the Swiss Brethren and was burned at Rottenburg)
German surname, ‘saddler.’ The Schleitheim articles of 24 February 1527 are named for the village where they were agreed.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Michael Sattler was prior of the Benedictine monastery of St Peter in the Black Forest when the Reformation reached him; he left, married a former Beguine named Margaretha, and joined the Swiss Brethren. At Schleitheim in February 1527 he drafted seven articles that became the founding statement of the movement: believer's baptism; the ban, or church discipline, after Christ's order, “go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone” (Mat 18:15); the breaking of bread among the baptized; separation from the world, “come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17); pastors chosen by the congregation; refusal of the sword to Christians; and refusal of all oaths, after Christ's word, “Swear not at all” (Mat 5:34). A few months later he was arrested, tried at Rottenburg, had his tongue cut and his flesh torn with hot tongs, and was burned on 21 May 1527; Margaretha was drowned. Even his enemies recorded his calm. The Particular Baptists of the 1689 Confession share his first three articles in substance, and part with him on the last two, confessing that a Christian may lawfully hold the magistrate's office and that a lawful oath is part of religious worship.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines oath as a solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.

expand to see more

OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.

2. The appeal to God in an oath implies that the person imprecates his vengeance and renounces his favour if the declaration is false.

Key Scripture

Mat 18:15 — "Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother."

2Co 6:17 — "Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,"

Mat 5:34 — "But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:"

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

Modern Corruption

The Schleitheim articles are now claimed as the charter of Christian pacifism and political withdrawal; a Baptist reading honours Sattler's church order and corrects his reading of the sword and the oath from Scripture.

expand to see more

Modern neo-Anabaptist theology treats Schleitheim's articles on the sword and the oath as the purest form of the Sermon on the Mount, and judges every Christian magistrate and soldier by them. But Christ's prohibition of swearing in Matthew 5 rebuked the casuistry that made some oaths binding and others not; it did not forbid the oath God Himself commanded in the law and swore by in the gospel. Paul calls the ruler God's minister bearing the sword (Rom 13:1–4) without telling Christian rulers to resign.

The recovery is to receive what was right at Schleitheim — a believers' church, real discipline, the Supper fenced, pastors chosen by the flock — and to confess with the 1689 Confession that a lawful oath is part of religious worship and that Christians may lawfully accept and execute the office of a magistrate. Sattler's courage under torture is to be honoured without inheriting his errors.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek elencho (G1651), to tell one's fault, convict; aphorizo (G873), to separate; omnuo (G3660), to swear.

expand to see more

Greek elencho (G1651) — to convict, rebuke; Matthew 18:15.

Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, set apart; 2 Corinthians 6:17.

Greek omnuo (G3660) — to swear, take an oath; Matthew 5:34, Hebrews 6:13, 16.

Usage

"“tell him his fault between thee and him alone” (Mat 18:15) — Schleitheim's article on the ban."

"“come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — the article on separation."

"“Swear not at all” (Mat 5:34) — the text Sattler read too broadly."
